claim: Primates use gaze cues to follow peer gaze to an object of joint attention.
source: Primates use gaze cues to follow peer gaze to an object of joint attention.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about primate behavior.

claim: Gaze following of monkeys is largely determined by head or face orientation.
source: Gaze following of monkeys is largely determined by head or face orientation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and is consistent with established knowledge about monkey gaze following.

claim: Head gaze following activated a distinct region in the posterior STS, close to-albeit not overlapping with-the medial face patch delineated by passive viewing of faces.
source: Head gaze following activated a distinct region in the posterior STS, close to-albeit not overlapping with-the medial face patch delineated by passive viewing of faces.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI experiments reported in the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: The 'gaze following patch' may be the substrate of the geometrical calculations needed to translate information on head orientation from the face patches into precise shifts of attention.
source: This 'gaze following patch' may be the substrate of the geometrical calculations needed to translate information on head orientation from the face patches into precise shifts of attention, taking the spatial relationship of the two interacting agents into account.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Successful social interactions require understanding of peer dispositions, desires, beliefs and intentions.
source: Successful social interactions require understanding of peer dispositions, desires, beliefs and intentions.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing from established knowledge in social cognition.

claim: A major step in developing theory of mind is our ability to shift our attention to the same location and/or object the other one is interested in, that is to establish joint attention.
source: A major step in developing this theory of (the other one's) mind (TOM) is our ability to shift our attention to the same location and/or object the other one is interested in, that is to establish joint attention (Baron-Cohen, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Baron-Cohen, 1995.

claim: In humans, the most important bodily cue for joint attention is peer eye gaze, which provides extremely precise spatial information.
source: In case of humans, arguably the most important bodily cue, reliably providing extremely precise spatial information (Bock et al., 2008), is peer eye gaze, a cue that can be easily retrieved even from quite some distance because of the high contrast border between the eye's dark center and periphery.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bock et al., 2008.

claim: The eyes of macaque monkeys and many other nonhuman primates lack comparable contrasts to human eyes.
source: The eyes of macaque monkeys and many other nonhuman primates (NHP) lack comparable contrasts (Kobayashi and Kohshima, 1997), which is why eye gaze seems to be of little importance in this group (Lorincz et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kobayashi and Kohshima, 1997 and Lorincz et al., 1999.

claim: Eye gaze is of little importance for joint attention in macaque monkeys and many other nonhuman primates.
source: The eyes of macaque monkeys and many other nonhuman primates (NHP) lack comparable contrasts (Kobayashi and Kohshima, 1997), which is why eye gaze seems to be of little importance in this group (Lorincz et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lorincz et al., 1999.

claim: Monkeys seem to lack a full-fledged theory of mind.
source: While monkeys seem to lack a full-fledged TOM (Anderson et al., 1996) (Flombaum and Santos, 2005 for a different view), they are nevertheless able to establish joint attention with conspecifics, largely relying on head gaze, that is the orientation of peer head (=face).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 1996, with a note that Flombaum and Santos, 2005 present a different view.

claim: Monkeys are able to establish joint attention with conspecifics, largely relying on head gaze.
source: While monkeys seem to lack a full-fledged TOM (Anderson et al., 1996) (Flombaum and Santos, 2005 for a different view), they are nevertheless able to establish joint attention with conspecifics, largely relying on head gaze, that is the orientation of peer head (=face).
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge and is consistent with the experimental design of the study.

claim: Not only human but also monkey gaze following seems to be geometric.
source: Importantly, not only human but also monkey gaze following seems to be geometric: the observer identifies peer focus of attention by following his/her gaze towards the object of interest (Emery et al., 1997; Emery, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Emery et al., 1997 and Emery, 2000.

claim: Geometrical gaze following implies that a gaze vector is defined which is used to search for the object of interest.
source: In other words, rather than simply using the directional information provided by a gaze cue to shift attention out from the center until an object of potential interest is encountered, geometrical gaze following implies that a gaze vector is defined which is used to search for the object of interest (Butterworth and Jarrett, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Butterworth and Jarrett, 1991.

claim: The gaze following of monkeys and man is dependent on social context.
source: Another important feature shared by the gaze following of monkeys and man is the dependence on social context.
evidence: This statement is supported by subsequent citations to Liuzza et al. (2011) and Shepherd et al. (2006).

claim: Human observers tend to prefer gaze cues of those whom they feel close to.
source: For instance, human observers tend to prefer gaze cues of those whom they feel close to Liuzza et al. (2011), while monkeys are particularly eager to follow the gaze of higher status conspecifics (Shepherd et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liuzza et al. (2011).

claim: Monkeys are particularly eager to follow the gaze of higher status conspecifics.
source: For instance, human observers tend to prefer gaze cues of those whom they feel close to Liuzza et al. (2011), while monkeys are particularly eager to follow the gaze of higher status conspecifics (Shepherd et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shepherd et al., 2006.

claim: Monkey and human gaze following may share homologous substrates, although the choice of the relevant social cue—eye vs head—differs.
source: The availability of geometric gaze following in monkeys and man and the modulatory influence of context supports the idea that monkey and human gaze following may actually be closely related, sharing homologous substrates, although the choice of the relevant social cue—eye vs head—differs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarities between monkey and human gaze following described in the text.

claim: The object position will have to be transformed from a demonstrator-centered frame of reference into an observer-centered frame of reference before a successful shift of attention can be programmed.
source: However, as this specific location will be an exception rather than the rule, the object position will have to be transformed from a demonstrator-centered frame of reference (FOR) into an observer-centered FOR before a successful shift of attention can be programmed.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the computational requirements of gaze following.

claim: Single unit recordings from monkey area LIP suggest that it is the major substrate of the shifts of attention which are prompted by social cues providing spatial information.
source: For instance, single unit recordings from monkey area LIP suggest that it is the major substrate of the shifts of attention which are prompted by social cues providing spatial information (Shepherd et al., 2009) as well as by non-social spatial cues (Bisley et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Shepherd et al., 2009 and Bisley et al., 2011.

claim: BOLD imaging studies of human cortex have consistently singled out an area in the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) specifically activated by the processing of eye gaze cues leading to subsequent shifts of attention.
source: On the other hand, BOLD imaging studies of human cortex have consistently singled out an area in the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) specifically activated by the processing of eye gaze cues leading to subsequent shifts of attention (Materna et al., 2008a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Materna et al., 2008a.

claim: BOLD imaging can delineate a patch of cortex in the monkey STS activated by head gaze following.
source: BOLD imaging is also able to delineate a patch of cortex in the monkey STS activated by head gaze following, arguably offering similar functionality as the human pSTS region and perhaps even being homologous (Kamphuis et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kamphuis et al., 2009.

claim: Previous work on face processing has established a set of six disparate but interconnected 'face patches' distributed along the rostro-caudal extent of the monkey STS.
source: This possibility is supported by the fact that previous work on face processing has established a set of six disparate but interconnected 'face patches' distributed along the rostro-caudal extent of the monkey STS, that is found in the same general region as the gaze following patch (Tsao et al., 2003, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tsao et al., 2003, 2008.

claim: Face patches form a hierarchically organized network with functionally specialized nodes.
source: As previous work on face processing has suggested that these face patches form a hierarchically organized network with functionally specialized nodes (Moeller et al., 2008; Freiwald and Tsao, 2010), we reasoned that one of these nodes might actually correspond to the gaze following patch.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Moeller et al., 2008 and Freiwald and Tsao, 2010.

claim: The gaze following patch is not part of the face patch network.
source: Using fMRI to delineate the passive face patch network and the gaze following patch in the same rhesus monkeys, we here show that, surprisingly, this expectation is not met. Rather than being part of the face patch network, the gaze following patch remains outside the network, albeit close to one of its nodes, the medial face patch.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: The gaze following patch is close to the medial face patch.
source: Rather than being part of the face patch network, the gaze following patch remains outside the network, albeit close to one of its nodes, the medial face patch.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: The accuracy levels were not significantly different in the gaze following and identity-matching tasks.
source: The accuracy levels were not significantly different in the two tasks (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Saccade latencies were not different between the gaze following and identity-matching tasks.
source: Saccade latencies were also not different (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: In each and every case the number of responses in the gaze following category by far surpassed the numbers in the two other categories.
source: In each and every case the number of responses in the gaze following category by far surpassed the numbers in the two other categories (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from control experiments presented in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The dominance of gaze following was statistically highly significant.
source: The dominance of gaze following was statistically highly significant (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data presented in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The observers M1 and M2 followed the gaze of the monkey portrait in the gaze following task.
source: These behavioral results clearly demonstrated that the observers M1 and M2 followed the gaze of the monkey portrait in the gaze following task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral control experiments.

claim: Analyzing the whole brain of M1 for the 'gaze following > identity matching' BOLD contrast, the only region showing a significant contrast was a patch of voxels located unilaterally on the lower bank of the right STS, between the interaural line and 2 mm posterior to it (A0-P2), near to the dorsal end of the inferior occipital sulcus.
source: Analyzing the whole brain of M1 for the 'gaze following > identity matching' BOLD contrast, the only region showing a significant contrast was a patch of voxels (='gaze following (GF) patch') located unilaterally on the lower bank of the right STS, between the interaural line and 2 mm posterior to it (A0-P2), near to the dorsal end of the inferior occipital sulcus (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The absence of a significant BOLD contrast on the left side in M1 might have been the consequence of a poorer signal-to-noise ratio on the left side, possibly due to the positioning of the eye-tracking camera in front of the left eye.
source: We reasoned that the absence of a significant BOLD contrast on the opposite site might have been the consequence of a poorer signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the left side, possibly due to the positioning of the eye-tracking camera in front of the left eye.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the unilateral BOLD pattern.

claim: Additional experiments in M1 with a focal coil centered on the posterior left STS did not obtain a significant BOLD contrast in the area sampled by the coil.
source: To test it, we performed additional experiments in M1 with a focal coil centered on the posterior left STS, expected to be less affected by the camera. Yet, also with this coil we did not obtain a significant BOLD contrast in the area sampled by the coil, which included the region corresponding to the activated GF patch on the opposite side.
evidence: This is a finding from additional fMRI experiments.

claim: The focal coil centered on the left STS allowed confirmation of the right posterior STS BOLD contrast obtained in a whole-brain analysis of the data collected with the bilateral coil.
source: Interestingly, despite the fact that the focal coil was centered on the left STS, it allowed us to confirm the right posterior STS BOLD contrast obtained in a whole-brain analysis of the data collected with the bilateral coil (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from additional fMRI experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The possibility that the unilateral BOLD pattern might be secondary to differences in the behavior directed at the two sides can be excluded.
source: Finally, also the possibility that the unilateral BOLD pattern might be secondary to differences in the behavior directed at the two sides can be excluded.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on behavioral analysis.

claim: A comparison of responses to the demonstrator's gaze directed to the left and to the right respectively did not reveal any differences in accuracy.
source: A comparison of responses to the demonstrator's gaze directed to the left and to the right respectively did not reveal any differences in accuracy ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data analysis described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In M2, a significant BOLD contrast for gaze following compared to identity matching was revealed in the lower bank of the STS on both sides, around 1 mm anterior to the interaural line (A1), near the dorsal end of the inferior temporal sulcus.
source: By this approach we revealed a significant BOLD contrast for gaze following compared to identity matching in the lower bank of the STS on both sides, around 1 mm anterior to the interaural line (A1), near the dorsal end of the inferior temporal sulcus (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI experiments in M2, supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The GF patch in the right hemisphere of M2 was shifted by 1–2 mm anterior to the coordinates of the GF patch in M1.
source: The GF patch in the right hemisphere of M2 was shifted by 1–2 mm anterior to the coordinates of the GF patch in M1.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the fMRI data from the two monkeys.

claim: The slight shift in the location of the GF patch between M1 and M2 is a manifestation of interindividual variability and does not question the spatial identity of the GF patch in the two monkeys.
source: This strongly suggests that the slight shift is a manifestation of interindividual variability and thus does not question the spatial identity of the GF patch in the two monkeys.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed differences in GF patch location.

claim: M2 in the left STS had 3 disparate patches of gaze following-associated BOLD.
source: However, it is harder to explain the fact that M2 in the left STS had 3 disparate patches of gaze following-associated BOLD.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments in M2.

claim: The posterior-most patch in the left STS of M2 exhibited a much stronger peak BOLD signal than the other two patches and corresponds to the GF patch on the right side in terms of coordinates.
source: In terms of their location, the posterior-most patch, which exhibited a much stronger peak BOLD signal than the other two, corresponds to the GF patch on the right side in terms of coordinates.
evidence: This is an observation from the fMRI data in M2.

claim: The peak BOLD responses of the two more anterior patches located in the left STS of M2, around A4 and A8 respectively, were much weaker, although consistent across the usage of the two different coil systems.
source: On the other hand, the peak BOLD responses of the two more anterior patches located in the left STS, around A4 and A8 respectively, were much weaker, although consistent across the usage of the two different coil systems.
evidence: This is an observation from the fMRI data in M2.

claim: For the 'identity matching > gaze following' BOLD contrast, significance was reached only at a level of p<0.05 (uncorrected).
source: For the 'identity matching > gaze following' BOLD contrast we reached significance only at a level of p<0.05 (uncorrected).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: In M1 the identity matching-related activity was found unilaterally on the lower lateral bank of the right STS around 17 mm anterior to the interaural line (A17).
source: In M1 the activity was found unilaterally on the lower lateral bank of the right STS around 17 mm anterior to the interaural line (A17).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments in M1.

claim: In M2 the identity matching-related activity was bilateral in the medial part of the STS around 22 mm anterior to the interaural line (A22).
source: In M2 it was bilateral in the medial part of the STS around 22 mm anterior to the interaural line (A22).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments in M2.

claim: A pattern of face-specific BOLD activations consisting of a number of distinct patches was identified, with coordinates and spatial layout corresponding to the face patches described by previous work.
source: Analyzing the whole brain of M1 and focusing on the temporal lobes of M2, we identified a pattern of face-specific BOLD activations consisting of a number of distinct patches. Their coordinates and their spatial layout corresponded to the face patches described by previous work (Tsao et al., 2003, 2008; Moeller et al., 2008) and at least partially confirmed by subsequent studies (Pinsk et al., 2005; Bell et al., 2009; Ku et al., 2011): three bilateral anterior face-patches (anterior medial, AM; anterior lateral, AL; anterior fundus, AF), two middle bilateral face-patches (middle lateral, ML and middle fundus, MF) and one bilateral posterior face patch (posterior lateral, PL) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 4 and citations to previous work.

claim: The results of face patch identification were consistent across the two monkeys and consistent across the two different receiver coil systems used in M2.
source: The results were consistent across the two monkeys and consistent across the two different receiver coil systems used in M2 (focal unilateral coil vs bilateral coil).
evidence: This is an observation about the consistency of the fMRI findings.

claim: The least clear face patches were AM, AF and PL, as the BOLD activation for those voxels reached significance only at a level of p<0.05 (uncorrected).
source: The least clear patches were AM, AF and PL, as the BOLD activation for those voxels reached significance only at a level of p<0.05 (uncorrected), whereas the other clusters (ML, MF and AL) reached significance already on a level of p<0.005 (uncorrected).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: The GF patch in the posterior STS did not overlap with any of the face patches identified.
source: The GF patch in the posterior STS did not overlap with any of the face patches we identified (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing the fMRI data from the two experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The GF patch was posterior (with respect to the interaural line) relative to the middle face patches (ML and MF) and anterior to the posterior face patch (PL).
source: Actually, the GF patch was posterior (with respect to the interaural line) relative to the middle face patches (ML and MF) and anterior to the posterior face patch (PL).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the locations of the GF patch and face patches.

claim: Despite the slight difference between the location of the GF patch in the two monkeys, the relative distance between this patch and the middle face patch (ML) matches in the two monkeys.
source: Moreover, despite the slight difference between the location of the GF patch in the two monkeys the relative distance between this patch and the middle face patch (ML) matches in the two monkeys.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the fMRI data from the two monkeys.

claim: The additional anterior gaze following patches found in the left hemisphere of M2 only, overlapped with the MF face patch in this monkey.
source: Unlike the major (posterior) GF patch, the additional anterior gaze following patches found in the left hemisphere of M2 only, overlapped with the MF face patch in this monkey.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the fMRI data from the two experiments in M2.

claim: The weak anterior patch found for the 'identity matching vs gaze following' contrast overlapped with anterior face patches.
source: Interestingly, the weak anterior patch we had found for the opposite, 'identity matching vs gaze following' contrast, overlapped with anterior face patches: in M1 the unilateral identity patch on the lower bank of the STS around A17 right overlapped with the anterior lateral face patch (AL) in this monkey. In M2 the bilateral identity patches on the medial part of the STS around A22 overlapped with the anterior medial face patch (AM).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the fMRI data from the two experiments.

claim: The experimental animals deployed geometrical head gaze following.
source: Hence, we can be sure that our experimental animals deployed geometrical head gaze following (Emery et al., 1997; Emery, 2000).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral control experiments, with citations to Emery et al., 1997 and Emery, 2000.

claim: The location of the GF patch in this study corresponds to cytoarchitectonic area TEO and area PITd.
source: Using gaze direction rather than identity to shift attention was associated with a distinct patch of BOLD activity (GF patch) in a region of the posterior STS, on its lower bank around A1-P1, near the dorsal end of the inferior temporal sulcus, corresponding to cytoarchitectonic area TEO (Bonin and Bailey, 1947; Ungerleider and Desimone, 1986) and area PITd, the latter defined based on topographic and connectional data (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GF patch location based on anatomical knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The location of the GF patch in this study is more posterior than BOLD activity interpreted as being gaze following related in two other monkeys used in a previous study by Kamphuis et al. (2009).
source: The location of the GF patch in this study is more posterior than BOLD activity, interpreted as being gaze following related, in two other monkeys used in a previous study by Kamphuis et al. (2009). In that study, gaze following-related activity was found between A4.4-6.4 in one animal and A0.8-A3.3 in the other one.
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from a previous study, supported by a citation to Kamphuis et al., 2009.

claim: The anterior deviation of the location of the gaze following activity in the second monkey of Kamphuis et al. relative to the GF patch in the present study is not much larger than the interindividual differences in the present study.
source: In other words, the anterior deviation of the location of the gaze following activity in the second monkey of Kamphuis et al. relative to the GF patch in the present study is not much larger than the interindividual differences in the present study (M1:A0-P2, M2: A2-P1).
evidence: This is a comparison of the present findings with those of Kamphuis et al.

claim: A limitation of the Kamphuis et al. study was that because of a lack of behavioral controls the authors could not exclude that the experimental animals might not have resorted to a workaround strategy based on learned associations between portraits and targets.
source: Actually, a limitation of the Kamphuis et al. study was that because of a lack of behavioral controls the authors could not exclude that the experimental animals might not have resorted to a workaround strategy based on learned associations between portraits and targets.
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of the Kamphuis et al. study.

claim: The two conditions compared in the Kamphuis et al. study in order to identify gaze following-related BOLD activity involved subtle visual differences.
source: Moreover, the two conditions compared in order to identify gaze following-related BOLD activity involved subtle visual differences.
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of the Kamphuis et al. study.

claim: The pattern evoked in the Kamphuis et al. study may have been influenced by variables other than gaze following.
source: Hence, a possibility is that the pattern evoked in the Kamphuis et al. study may have been influenced by variables other than gaze following and we may speculate that these variables may have played a larger role in the odd monkey.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differences between the present study and Kamphuis et al.

claim: In one monkey the GF patch could be delineated bilaterally in the STS in corresponding locations.
source: Whereas in one monkey the GF patch could be delineated bilaterally in the STS in corresponding locations, much to our surprise, the gaze following-related activity in the other monkey was confined to the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments.

claim: The gaze following-related activity in one monkey was confined to the right hemisphere.
source: Whereas in one monkey the GF patch could be delineated bilaterally in the STS in corresponding locations, much to our surprise, the gaze following-related activity in the other monkey was confined to the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments.

claim: Attempts to lead the unilaterality of gaze following-related activity back to differences in the quality of the MRI signal on the two sides or to differences in the behavior directed at the two sides, failed.
source: Our attempts to lead this unilaterality back to differences in the quality of the MRI signal on the two sides or to differences in the behavior directed at the two sides, failed.
evidence: This is a statement about the results of additional analyses.

claim: The unilaterality of gaze following-related activity seems specific to gaze following as testing the same monkey in a passive face perception task to delineate the face patch network did not reveal any major hemispheric differences.
source: Whatever the reason for the unilaterality may be, it seems specific to gaze following as testing the same monkey in a passive face perception task to delineate the face patch network did not reveal any major hemispheric differences.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the results of the two experiments.

claim: Previous behavioral studies on gaze following in healthy human subjects and patients with lesions support a specific role of the right hemisphere in gaze following and social cognition in general.
source: Previous behavioral studies on gaze following in healthy human subjects and patients with lesions (Ricciardelli et al., 2002; Akiyama et al., 2006a, 2006b) supports a specific role of the right hemisphere in gaze following and social cognition in general (Brancucci et al., 2009 for review).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ricciardelli et al., 2002; Akiyama et al., 2006a, 2006b; and Brancucci et al., 2009.

claim: fMRI studies of gaze following in humans have yielded mixed results, with some showing mainly right hemisphere STS activation and others bilateral pSTS activation.
source: On the other hand, fMRI studies of gaze following in humans have yielded mixed results, with some showing mainly right hemisphere STS activation (Pelphrey et al., 2003, 2004, 2005; Calder et al., 2007; Laube et al., 2011) and others bilateral pSTS activation (Puce et al., 1998; Hoffman and Haxby, 2000; Materna et al., 2008a, 2008b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple fMRI studies.

claim: It is tempting to see certain analogies between the human data and the monkey findings and to conclude that gaze following in monkeys and man may in principal be bihemispheric, though the substrates on the left side are deployed to individually varying degrees.
source: Hence, it is tempting to see certain analogies between the human data and our monkey findings and to conclude that gaze following in monkeys and man may in principal be bihemispheric, though the substrates on the left side are deployed to individually varying degrees.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of human studies.

claim: The idea of true hemispheric differences in monkeys receives further support from the fact that the left STS of monkey M2 not only showed a GF patch with coordinates matching those of the patch in the right hemisphere but in addition two more anterior patches without equivalents in the right hemisphere of this monkey and none of the two hemispheres of monkey M1.
source: The idea of true hemispheric differences in monkeys receives further support from the fact that the left STS of monkey M2 not only showed a GF patch with coordinates matching those of the patch in the right hemisphere but in addition two more anterior patches without equivalents in the right hemisphere of this monkey and none of the two hemispheres of monkey M1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings.

claim: Recent work on audio-vocal communication in macaque monkeys emphasizes an advantage of the left hemisphere.
source: Actually, recent work on audio-vocal communication in macaque monkeys, emphasizing an advantage of the left hemisphere (Heffner and Heffner, 1984; Ghazanfar and Hauser, 2001; Poremba et al., 2004), supports the idea that there is some hemispheric specialization in macaque monkeys.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Heffner and Heffner, 1984; Ghazanfar and Hauser, 2001; and Poremba et al., 2004.

claim: There is some hemispheric specialization in macaque monkeys.
source: Actually, recent work on audio-vocal communication in macaque monkeys, emphasizing an advantage of the left hemisphere (Heffner and Heffner, 1984; Ghazanfar and Hauser, 2001; Poremba et al., 2004), supports the idea that there is some hemispheric specialization in macaque monkeys.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous work.

claim: More subjects will have to be studied to decide if the seeming unilaterality in monkey M1 is more than an idiosyncrasy.
source: In any case, more subjects will have to be studied to decide if the seeming unilaterality in monkey M1 is more than an idiosyncrasy.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study and future research needs.

claim: The only difference with respect to the later studies of Tsao et al. was a somewhat weaker and less consistent activation of the anterior and posterior face patches.
source: The only difference with respect to the later studies of Tsao et al. (Moeller et al., 2008; Tsao et al., 2008) was a somewhat weaker and less consistent activation of the anterior and posterior face patches.
evidence: This is a comparison of the present findings with those of previous studies.

claim: The weaker and less consistent activation of the anterior and posterior face patches is most probably a consequence of methodological differences.
source: This difference is most probably a consequence of methodological differences: these later studies (Moeller et al., 2008; Tsao et al., 2008) relied on MION-based measurements of activity-related changes in blood volume, well-known to be more sensitive by a factor of 3 than the BOLD method deployed by us, using the same 3T scanner (Leite et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differences, supported by a citation to Leite et al., 2002.

claim: MION-based measurements of activity-related changes in blood volume are more sensitive by a factor of 3 than the BOLD method.
source: This difference is most probably a consequence of methodological differences: these later studies (Moeller et al., 2008; Tsao et al., 2008) relied on MION-based measurements of activity-related changes in blood volume, well-known to be more sensitive by a factor of 3 than the BOLD method deployed by us, using the same 3T scanner (Leite et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Leite et al., 2002.

claim: When relying on BOLD imaging of the monkey face patch system and deploying a comparably high significance threshold, an earlier study of Tsao et al. identified only a fraction of the face patches which were later demonstrated with MION.
source: Actually, when relying on BOLD imaging of the monkey face patch system and deploying a comparably high significance threshold, also an earlier study of Tsao et al. (2003) identified only a fraction of the face patches which were later demonstrated with MION.
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from a previous study, supported by a citation to Tsao et al., 2003.

claim: In the earlier BOLD study of Tsao et al., the strongest activity was found in the face patches in the fundus and lower bank of the middle STS (corresponding to ML and MF) and the face-patch located in rostral TE (corresponding to AL).
source: In this earlier study the strongest activity was found in the face patches in the fundus and lower bank of the middle STS (corresponding to ML and MF in Moeller et al., 2008; Tsao et al., 2008) and the face-patch located in rostral TE (corresponding to AL in Moeller et al., 2008; Tsao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from a previous study, supported by citations.

claim: In the earlier BOLD study of Tsao et al., the patch in the STS in area TEO (corresponding to PL) was not reliable across different days and other anterior face patches (AF and AM) were not reported.
source: The patch in the STS in area TEO (corresponding to PL in Moeller et al., 2008; Tsao et al., 2008) was not reliable across different days and other anterior face patches (AF and AM) were not reported.
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from a previous study, supported by citations.

claim: All the medial and posterior face patches described before were clearly identified, which were in the vicinity of the GF patch.
source: Nevertheless, we clearly identified all the medial and posterior face patches described before (Moeller et al., 2008; Tsao et al., 2008) which were in the vicinity of our GF patch.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings, supported by citations.

claim: The complete separation of the GF patch from any of the neighboring face patches with ML/MF being closest to the GF patch is a major finding.
source: This is important as our major finding is the complete separation of the GF patch from any of the neighboring face patches with ML/MF being closest to the GF patch.
evidence: This is a statement emphasizing the importance of a primary finding.

claim: The face patch system in monkeys is largely bilateral.
source: The face patch system in monkeys is largely bilateral (Tsao et al., 2003, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tsao et al., 2003, 2008.

claim: The fact that unlike face-related activity, the gaze following-related activity was unilateral in one of the two monkeys studied, further supports the notion of two distinct and anatomically separated systems.
source: The fact that unlike face-related activity, the gaze following-related activity was unilateral in one of the two monkeys studied, further supports the notion of two distinct and anatomically separated systems.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The two weak BOLD responses observed inconsistently much more anterior in conjunction with gaze following overlapped with the MF face patch.
source: On the other hand, the two weak BOLD responses observed inconsistently much more anterior in conjunction with gaze following overlapped with the MF face patch.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments.

claim: The overlap of anterior gaze following-related BOLD with the MF face patch may suggest that MF may be more important for processing information on facial orientation than on facial identity.
source: This overlap may suggest that MF may be more important for processing information on facial orientation than on facial identity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the overlap.

claim: Physical proximity does not necessarily imply connectivity and close functional relationship.
source: Physical proximity does not necessarily imply connectivity and close functional relationship.
evidence: This is a general statement based on knowledge of neuroscience.

claim: Many face-selective cells in ML/MF are tuned to specific face (=head) orientations.
source: Yet, the properties of neurons in ML/MF are suggestive of a functional relationship: many face-selective cells are tuned to specific face (=head) orientations (Freiwald et al., 2009; Freiwald and Tsao, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Freiwald et al., 2009 and Freiwald and Tsao, 2010.

claim: The information on head orientation is exactly the kind of information head gaze following builds on.
source: This is exactly the kind of information head gaze following builds on.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between head orientation information and gaze following.

claim: To identify the goal of the other one's gaze in the frame of reference of the observer or in a world-centered frame of reference shared by both agents, the spatial relationship of the two agents and the relationship of potential goal objects relative to the two agents needs to be taken into account.
source: To identify the goal of the other one's gaze in the frame of reference of the observer or, alternatively, in a world-centered frame of reference shared by both agents, the spatial relationship of the two agents and the relationship of potential goal objects relative to the two agents needs to be taken into account also.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the computational requirements of gaze following.

claim: The GF patch could be the substrate of the geometrical calculations needed to establish the goal representation, adding the required contextual information to the elementary face (=head) orientation information taken over from the ML/MF.
source: Hence, it is intriguing to speculate that the GF patch could be the substrate of the geometrical calculations needed to establish this goal representation, to this end adding the required contextual information to the elementary face (=head) orientation information taken over from the ML/MF (Freiwald et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of the GF patch, with a citation to Freiwald et al., 2009.

claim: Microstimulation of parietal area LIP causes stimulation-induced BOLD responses in a part of the STS whose coordinates seem to correspond to those of the GF patch.
source: This idea receives additional support from the fact that microstimulation of parietal area LIP causes stimulation-induced BOLD responses in a part of the STS whose coordinates seem to correspond to those of our study GF patch (Crapse et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Crapse et al., 2013.

claim: Area LIP is a well-established center of overt and covert shifts of attention guided by a wide variety of cues, including head gaze.
source: Area LIP is a well-established center of overt and covert shifts of attention guided by a wide variety of cues, including head gaze (Shepherd et al., 2009; Bisley et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Shepherd et al., 2009 and Bisley et al., 2011.

claim: Using a comparable approach to delineate the cortical substrates of eye gaze following in humans, gaze following related BOLD activity was described bilaterally in the posterior STS ('pSTS region').
source: Using a comparable approach to delineate the cortical substrates of eye gaze following in humans, gaze following related BOLD activity was described bilaterally in the posterior STS ('pSTS region') (Materna et al., 2008a), later shown to be activated also by following other biological cues like finger pointing (Materna et al., 2008b) and head orientation (Laube et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Materna et al., 2008a, 2008b and Laube et al., 2011.

claim: The pSTS region in humans was shown to be activated also by following other biological cues like finger pointing and head orientation.
source: Using a comparable approach to delineate the cortical substrates of eye gaze following in humans, gaze following related BOLD activity was described bilaterally in the posterior STS ('pSTS region') (Materna et al., 2008a), later shown to be activated also by following other biological cues like finger pointing (Materna et al., 2008b) and head orientation (Laube et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Materna et al., 2008b and Laube et al., 2011.

claim: Presenting distracting eye gaze cue in conjunction with head gaze following led to a clear modulation of the BOLD signal in the pSTS.
source: Importantly, presenting distracting eye gaze cue in conjunction with head gaze following led to a clear modulation of the BOLD signal in the pSTS (Laube et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Laube et al., 2011.

claim: Monkeys seem to pay very little attention to the other one's eye when trying to establish joint attention.
source: This must not be expected in view of the fact that monkeys seem to pay very little attention to the other one's eye when trying to establish joint attention.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about monkey behavior.

claim: Independent of the differing weights attributed to eye and head gaze in humans and monkeys, the geometrical calculations needed to pinpoint a spatial goal shared by the two interacting agents are comparable.
source: However, independent of the differing weights attributed to eye and head gaze in humans and monkeys, the geometrical calculations needed to pinpoint a spatial goal shared by the two interacting agents are comparable.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the computational requirements of gaze following.

claim: The regions in the monkey and human STS activated by gaze following may be analogous and possibly even homologous.
source: This consideration may suggest that the regions in the monkey and human STS activated by gaze following are analogous and possibly even homologous.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the relationship between monkey and human gaze following substrates.

claim: The BOLD activity related to the usage of facial identity for target localization in the anterior parts of the STS overlapped with activity evoked by the passive observation of faces.
source: In contrast to the absence of overlap between the GF patch and the neighboring face patches, the BOLD activity related to the usage of facial identity for target localization in the anterior parts of the STS overlapped with activity evoked by the passive observation of faces.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the fMRI data from the two experiments.

claim: The identity-associated signal coincided with AM in M2 and AL in M1.
source: The identity-associated signal coincided with AM in M2 and AL in M1.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI experiments.

claim: The anterior location of the identity matching BOLD activation fits the previous electrophysiological finding of identity-selective neurons in the anterior inferotemporal gyrus.
source: The anterior location of our identity matching BOLD activation fits the previous electrophysiological finding of identity-selective neurons in the anterior inferotemporal gyrus (Hasselmo et al., 1989; Eifuku et al., 2004; Freiwald and Tsao, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hasselmo et al., 1989; Eifuku et al., 2004; and Freiwald and Tsao, 2010.

claim: The percept of facial identity is disrupted by microstimulation of AM (and ML) face patches.
source: In accordance with the notion that these patches are involved in establishing facial identity, it was recently demonstrated that the percept of facial identity is disrupted by microstimulation of AM (and ML) face patches (Moeller and Tsao, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Moeller and Tsao, 2013.

claim: By requiring monkeys to use head gaze to locate spatial targets, a highly specific region in the posterior STS (GF patch) well separated from those parts of the STS known to process visual information on faces and heads was identified.
source: In summary, by requiring monkeys to use head gaze to locate spatial targets we could identify a highly specific region in the posterior STS (GF patch) well separated from those parts of the STS known to process visual information on faces and heads.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: The GF patch may correspond to the pSTS of humans devoted to eye gaze following.
source: We propose that this region corresponds to the pSTS of humans devoted to eye gaze following.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings.

claim: The GF patch may be the substrate of the geometrical calculations needed to translate head orientation into precise shifts of attention.
source: We furthermore suggest that this region may be the substrate of the geometrical calculations needed to translate head orientation into precise shifts of attention.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the function of the GF patch.

claim: Two rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) were used as subjects: monkey M1 (6 years, 8 kg) and monkey M2 (8 years, 11 kg).
source: Two rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta): monkey M1 (6 years, 8 kg); monkey M2 (8 years, 11 kg) were implanted with three cf-PEEK (carbon-fiber-enforced polyetheretherketone) tripods, each attached to the skull with six ceramic screws (Thomas Recording).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Surgeries were carried out under combination anesthesia with isoflurane and remifentanyl with monitoring of all relevant vital parameters.
source: Surgeries were carried out under combination anesthesia with isoflurane and remifentanyl with monitoring of all relevant vital parameters (body temperature, CO2, blood oxygen saturation, blood pressure, ECG).
evidence: This is a description of the surgical procedures.

claim: After surgery, monkeys were supplied with opioid analgesics (buprenorphin) until they fully recovered.
source: After surgery, monkeys were supplied with opioid analgesics (buprenorphin) until they fully recovered.
evidence: This is a description of post-surgical care.

claim: The study was performed in strict accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health.
source: The study was performed in strict accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

source: All of the animals were handled according to the guidelines of the German law regulating the usage of experimental animals and the protocols approved by the local institution in charge of experiments using animals (Regierungspraesidium Tuebingen, Abteilung Tierschutz, permit-number N1/08).

claim: Eye position was tracked in real time using a scanner-compatible low-cost CMOS-infra-red camera with infra-red emitting LEDs illuminating the monkey's eyes.

evidence: This is a description of the eye tracking methodology.

claim: The custom-made software running on a standard PC determined orientation of the center of the pupil with a spatial resolution of 0.5° visual angle and a temporal resolution of 50 Hz.
source: The custom-made software running on a standard PC determined orientation of the center of the pupil with a spatial resolution of 0.5° visual angle and a temporal resolution of 50 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the eye tracking methodology.

claim: Monkeys were scanned in a horizontal clinical scanner, 3T MRT (Trio, Siemens, Erlangen, Germany).
source: Monkeys were scanned in a horizontal clinical scanner, 3T MRT (Trio, Siemens, Erlangen, Germany).
evidence: This is a description of the MRI scanner used.

claim: Functional images were acquired using two custom-made linear receiver surface coils or one small surface coil.
source: Functional images were acquired using two custom-made linear receiver surface coils (diameter 13 cm, 'Helmholtz-configuration'; whole-brain scanning in M1 and STS-ROI scanning in M2, later referred as 'bilateral coil') or one small surface coil (diameter 3 cm; STS-ROI scanning in M2 and additional left STS-ROI scanning in M1, later referred as 'focal coil'), placed above the temporal lobe (centered on the posterior STS).
evidence: This is a description of the MRI coils used.
